description: SaxenaWave is a solo team by Ratnesh Saxena building MoonWindow, a lunar observation-window planner for Moon viewing sites, for the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge.
summary: MoonWindow is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare eight lunar landing sites for any date in 2027, visualising the Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation relative to the horizon to assess sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth line-of-sight windows. All astronomical values were computed by NASA JPL Horizons (DE441 ephemeris) from 48 live API queries made during the build and stored as data files; the tool runs entirely in the browser with no live API calls. It answers the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge (Challenge 10 – CLPS) by turning raw ephemeris data into a clear, comparable answer: which site, on which date, has sunlight and can see Earth. Built solo by Ratnesh Saxena (Team SaxenaWave, Mumbai Virtual).
details: The problem At the lunar south pole the Sun barely climbs above the horizon and Earth sits low in the sky, or below it, so whether a landing site gets sunlight — and whether it can see Earth — decides whether a mission can power itself and talk to home. Landing-site choice therefore depends on sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth line of sight, not just on terrain. The tool MoonWindow is a web tool (a static single-page web app in HTML/JavaScript, no server) that compares eight sourced lunar landing sites — Shackleton, Mons Mouton, Mons Malapert, Haworth, Nobile, Schrödinger Basin, Mare Crisium / Mons Latreille, and Gruithuisen Domes (Gamma) — for any date in 2027. For each site it shows daylight %, Earth-visible %, both-visible %, longest sunlit stretch, next sunrise and next Earthrise over the next lunar day (29.53 days). It has an A/B sky view with a 6-hour time slider, a 7-day visibility ribbon and a schematic 2D map. It answers the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge (Challenge 10 – CLPS) by turning raw ephemeris data into a clear, comparable answer: which site, on which date, has sunlight and can see Earth. Data and method All astronomical values — Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation — were computed by NASA JPL Horizons (DE441 ephemeris) from 48 live API queries made during the build and stored as data files; the tool runs entirely in the browser with no live API calls. Raw data was queried at 1-hour steps and is served as 6-hour series and daily metrics, and 32/32 spot-checks against raw Horizons output passed. Site coordinates are IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature feature centres, except the Blue Ghost 1 landing coordinate (NASA LRO/LROC). No ISRO data was used. Headline result Shackleton has 100.0% daylight over the next lunar day from 2027-01-01, with the longest continuous sunlit stretch of 4,015 hours / 167.3 days, 2027-08-06 to 2028-01-20. Earth visibility is 43.4% at Shackleton versus 0.0% at Schrödinger Basin — the same date can be a good landing window at one site and useless at another. Limitations The tool uses an ideal flat-horizon model: elevation greater than 0 degrees counts as visible. Local crater rims and ridges are not modelled. Version 1 uses no LOLA terrain and no NASA SVS Moon textures. It is an educational screening prototype, not flight-planning software. Links Live tool: https://rsaxena3011.github.io/moonwindow/ Source code (public, Apache 2.0): https://github.com/rsaxena3011/moonwindow Use of Super Intelligence (AI) NASA supplied the challenge brief. MoonWindow is our implementation. AI-assisted tools helped draft and debug code and explore interface design; no AI generated any data value, and no AI-generated images are used. This is an educational screening prototype, not flight-planning software: it estimates geometric sunlight and Earth line-of-sight, not power output, link budgets, or landing safety.
